newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavaria deal seals fate of unpopular sick pay cuts.
newsitem.headline: Bavaria deal seals fate of unpopular sick pay cuts.

text.p: The German engineering industry on Thursday struck another big regional wage accord guaranteeing full pay during sickness, sealing the fate of plans to implement an unpopular law allowing cuts in sick pay.
Metal and engineering employers in the southern state of Bavaria said they reached a wage deal with the IG Metall trade union, averting strikes threatened for the region.

The deal, which covers 650,000 workers, means the majority of Germany's 3.2 million engineering workers have succeeded in heading off a 20 percent cut in sick pay following a campaign of demonstrations and walkouts.
The law, which came into force last October, was originially seen as a gift from Chancellor Helmut Kohl to employers who have long bemoaned Germany's high labour costs.
But employers in both the engineering and banking sectors, faced with fierce worker resistance, have been unable to push the cuts through.

The chemical sector trade union IG Chemie, which represents around 590,000 workers, said employers were now ready to resume wage talks next week, a sign that full sick pay may be maintained in that industry as well.
The head of the Federation of German Chambers of Commerce (DIHT), Hans Peter Stihl, attacked employers for backing down, saying they were unable to conduct an industrial fight.
"The employers are evidently not able to organise a lockout in order to respond to strike action," Stihl told the Hamburger Abendblatt newspaper in an interview to be published on Friday.

Hundreds of thousands of workers have staged walkouts in recent months in defence of full sick pay, determined not to give up a privilege won by an earlier generation through strike action in the 1950s.
"The government and employers totally miscalculated the situation and fell flat on their faces," IG Metall spokeswoman Nele Loew Beer said.

The Bavaria deal set pay rises of 1.5 percent from April 1 next year and 2.5 percent from April 1998. That is similar to accords reached on Wednesday in the sector's largest region, North Rhine-Westphalia, which has 850,000 workers, and in the southern part of the state of Baden-Wuerrtemberg.
Talks with employers had been deadlocked until a breakthrough was reached last Thursday in the northern state of Lower Saxony, offering workers continued full sick pay and modest wage gains.
Rainer Hildmann, chief negotiator for the Bavarian employers, told journalists the Bavarian package "was not a good agreement" with terms largely dictated by those of the Lower Saxony accord.

Like other regional deals, the Bavaria agreement cuts workers' Christmas bonus to 55 percent from 60 percent of pay. Also, overtime payments will no longer be taken into account when calculating sick pay.

Further talks have been set in other regions. Negotiations for 60,000 engineering workers in western Berlin started on Thursday and talks for more than 400,000 workers in the states of Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland are set for December 18.
Talks will also be held for the northern part of the state of Baden-Wuerrtemberg and for the coastal region covering Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg, Bremen and the northwestern part of Lower Saxony.
